text: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Phobos orbits so close that it circles the planet three times a day. It is slowly spiralling inwards and may break into a ring in tens of millions of years.
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets. Its day is longer than its year: one rotation takes 243 Earth days, while one orbit of the Sun takes 225.
A day on Mars lasts about 24 hours and 39 minutes. Mission teams call it a sol. Rover operators on Earth shift their working hours every day to stay in step with the rover.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system. More than 1,300 Earths would fit inside it. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been watched since at least the 1830s.
The rover Perseverance landed on Mars in February 2021, in Jezero Crater. The crater once held a lake. The rover collects rock cores in sealed tubes for a future mission to bring back.
Saturn's rings are mostly made of ice, with some rock and dust. They are hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide but often only about ten metres thick.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun but not the hottest. With almost no atmosphere, its night side drops to about minus 180 degrees Celsius.
Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465 degrees Celsius at the surface. A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, and the pressure is about 90 times that on Earth.
Earth's Moon is slowly moving away, about 3.8 centimetres a year. Laser reflectors left by Apollo crews let scientists measure the distance precisely.
Uranus rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees. Each pole gets around 42 years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.
Neptune has the fastest winds measured in the solar system, above 2,000 kilometres per hour. It was found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. The New Horizons probe flew past it in 2015 and found a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice.
Europa, a moon of Jupiter, likely hides a salty ocean under its ice shell. The Europa Clipper spacecraft launched in October 2024 to study whether it could support life.
Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has lakes of liquid methane and ethane. It is the only moon with a thick atmosphere. The Dragonfly drone mission is planned to fly there.
Enceladus sprays jets of water vapour from cracks near its south pole. The Cassini probe flew through the plumes and detected salts and organic molecules.
Io is the most volcanically active body known. Tides from Jupiter flex its interior, heating it enough to power hundreds of active volcanoes.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Despite films, it is mostly empty space: the average distance between large asteroids is about a million kilometres.
Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and counts as a dwarf planet. The Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits in Occator Crater.
The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass. Light from its surface takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach Earth.
Solar flares can disrupt radio communications and GPS on Earth. Strong events also produce auroras far from the poles, as in May 2024.
Comets are icy bodies that grow tails when they near the Sun. The tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind.
Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years. It last passed in 1986 and is expected back in 2061.
The Voyager 1 probe launched in 1977 and is the most distant human-made object. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and still sends weak signals.
The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021. It observes in infrared from a point about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth called L2.
The Hubble Space Telescope has orbited Earth since 1990. Astronauts serviced it five times, the last in 2009.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometres up and circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes. People have lived on board continuously since November 2000.
A light-year is a distance, not a time: about 9.46 trillion kilometres. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light-years away.
Exoplanets are planets around other stars. More than 5,000 have been confirmed, many found by watching a star dim slightly as a planet passes in front.
The TRAPPIST-1 system has seven Earth-sized planets around a small, cool star. Several orbit in the zone where liquid water could exist.
Black holes form when massive stars collapse. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of one, in the galaxy M87.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun takes about 230 million years to orbit its centre.
The Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large galaxy to ours, about 2.5 million light-years away. It is expected to merge with the Milky Way in a few billion years.
Mars once had liquid water on its surface. Dry river valleys, deltas and minerals that form in water are visible from orbit.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest volcano in the solar system, about 22 kilometres high. Its base is roughly the size of Poland.
Valles Marineris is a canyon system on Mars about 4,000 kilometres long. It would stretch across most of the United States.
The Curiosity rover landed on Mars in August 2012 using a sky crane. It is still exploring Gale Crater and climbing Mount Sharp.
The Ingenuity helicopter made the first powered flight on another planet in April 2021. It flew 72 times before a damaged rotor ended its mission in January 2024.
Martian dust storms can cover the whole planet for weeks. A storm in 2018 blocked sunlight and ended the solar-powered Opportunity rover's mission.
A Martian year lasts 687 Earth days. Seasons there are almost twice as long as on Earth because of the longer orbit.
Gravity on Mars is about 38 percent of Earth's. A person weighing 70 kilograms on Earth would feel like 27 kilograms there.
Radio signals between Earth and Mars take between about 3 and 22 minutes one way. Rovers cannot be driven live and must follow planned commands.
Jupiter has the strongest magnetic field of any planet. Its radiation belts are dangerous to spacecraft electronics, so probes like Juno carry shielding.
The Juno spacecraft has orbited Jupiter since 2016. It found that the Great Red Spot reaches hundreds of kilometres down into the atmosphere.
Saturn is less dense than water. In theory it would float in a bathtub big enough to hold it.
The Cassini mission orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017. It ended by diving into the planet so it could not contaminate moons that might host life.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through dust left by comets. The Perseids peak each August and come from Comet Swift-Tuttle.
The Kuiper Belt is a region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Pluto and the object Arrokoth, visited by New Horizons in 2019, live there.
Space is not completely silent to instruments: plasma waves can be recorded and turned into sound. In air-free space, though, sound cannot travel between objects.
Rocket launches must account for Earth's rotation. Launching eastward near the equator gives a free boost of about 1,670 kilometres per hour.
